tools.what: Solve the break-even quantity from fixed cost, price and variable cost.
tools.formula: Break-even quantity = fixed cost / (price - variable cost per unit); break-even revenue = quantity x price; margin of safety = expected units - break-even units.
steps: Subtract variable cost from price to get the unit contribution and the contribution-margin ratio.
Divide fixed cost by the unit contribution for the break-even quantity.
Multiply by the price for the break-even revenue.
If you declare an expected volume, read the margin of safety; a profit target gives its volume.
common_mistakes: Using total cost instead of fixed cost.
Forgetting that a price below variable cost has no break-even.
Mixing per-unit and total figures.
Reporting a margin of safety against a budget you did not declare.

tools.label: Multi-product break-even
tools.what: Find the sales mix at which several products together cover their fixed costs.
tools.formula: Weighted contribution = sum(mix weight x unit contribution); break-even units = fixed cost / weighted contribution.
steps: Compute each product's unit contribution.
Weight the contributions by the declared sales mix.
Divide fixed cost by the weighted contribution.
Split the break-even units back across the mix.
common_mistakes: Using a simple average instead of the mix-weighted contribution.
Letting the mix change while claiming one break-even point.
Ignoring capacity limits.

tools.label: Check a trial balance
tools.what: Compare your own trial balance with the one your journal rebuilds to, and see every line that differs or is missing.
tools.formula: A trial balance balances when total debits equal total credits; the check compares each line with the one your own journal rebuilds.
steps: Paste the trial balance you prepared.
Paste the journal it came from, one dated balanced entry at a time.
Read every line that agrees, differs or has no counterpart.
Fix the entry the hint points to, not the total.
common_mistakes: Assuming a balanced trial balance proves the entries are right: a wrong account still balances.
Listing the same account twice with different figures.
Comparing a period-end balance with a movement.
Using the out-of-balance hint as the only diagnosis.

tools.label: Standard-cost variances
tools.what: Material price and usage, labour rate and efficiency, and overhead variances for the output produced.
tools.formula: Price = AQ(AP - SP); usage = SP(AQ - SQ); rate = AH(AR - SR); efficiency = SR(AH - SH); a positive variance is unfavourable.
steps: Enter the actual output and the standard quantity and price (or hours and rate) per unit.
Enter the actual quantity or hours and the actual price or rate.
Read each variance and its total; positive means actual cost exceeded the standard.
If you declare overhead, read the spending and efficiency (or volume) variances too.
common_mistakes: Using the actual output in the standard quantity but a budgeted output in the price variance.
Reversing the sign convention and calling an overspend favourable.
Forgetting that the usage variance is priced at the standard price.
Comparing variances across periods with different standards.

tools.label: Activity-based costing
tools.what: Activity rates, each product's allocation and its unit cost from the drivers it consumes.
tools.formula: Rate = pool cost / driver total; product allocation = sum of driver quantity x rate; unit cost = allocation / units.
steps: List the activity pools and their costs.
List the products and their units.
For each activity and product, declare the driver quantity consumed.
Read the rates, the allocations and the unit costs; every pool is allocated in full.
common_mistakes: Leaving an activity with a cost and no driver quantity.
Mixing driver units (setups and machine hours) in one pool.
Ignoring unused capacity, which stays in the pool and overstates unit cost.
Comparing an ABC unit cost with a traditional cost without saying which overhead was included.

tools.label: Sales price, mix and yield variances
tools.what: Reconcile the revenue change into price, mix and yield, per product and in total.
tools.formula: Price = actual units x (actual price - budget price); mix = budget price x (actual units - standard-mix units); yield = budget price x (standard-mix units - budget units).
steps: Enter budget and actual units and prices for two or more products.
Read the price, mix and yield variances per product and in total.
Check that they reconstruct the total revenue change.
Explain the movements from evidence outside the numbers, not from the variances alone.
common_mistakes: Adding price and volume without splitting mix and yield.
Using actual prices to value the mix variance.
Ignoring that a favourable price variance can come from a mix shift.
Comparing periods with different product sets.

tools.label: Tax on declared rates
tools.what: Income tax, VAT payable and deferred tax from the rates you declare, with the total charge.
tools.formula: Income tax = positive taxable income x declared rate; VAT payable = output tax - input tax; deferred tax = temporary difference x declared rate; total charge = income tax + deferred tax.
steps: Enter the taxable income you are declaring and the income tax rate as a decimal.
If the assignment includes VAT, enter the output and input tax.
If it includes deferred tax, enter the temporary difference and the rate.
Read the current tax, the VAT payable, the deferred tax and the total charge.
common_mistakes: Applying a national rate you have not declared or verified.
Treating a VAT credit (negative payable) as a refund.
Using accounting profit as taxable income without the adjustments.
Adding deferred tax to the cash tax paid.

tools.label: Working capital and EOQ
tools.what: Cash conversion cycle, order quantity, reorder point and the cost of forgoing a discount.
tools.formula: CCC = DSO + DIO - DPO; EOQ = square root of (2 x annual demand x order cost / holding cost per unit).
steps: Enter revenue, cost of sales and the three working-capital balances.
Read DSO, DIO, DPO and the cash conversion cycle.
Enter annual demand, order cost and holding cost for the order quantity.
Read the reorder point and the annualised cost of forgoing the trade discount.
common_mistakes: Using revenue for inventory days and payable days; those use cost of sales.
Treating the cash conversion cycle as a profitability measure.
Thinking the EOQ minimises purchase cost; it minimises order plus holding cost.
Comparing a discount cost with a borrowing rate without annualising both.

tools.label: Loan amortization
tools.what: Find the level payment, total interest and first-payment split on a fixed-rate loan.
tools.formula: PMT = P x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n), where r is the annual rate divided by payments per year and n is years x payments per year.
steps: Enter the principal, the nominal annual rate, the term and the payment frequency.
Convert the annual rate and the term to the payment period.
Read the level payment, then total paid and total interest.
Check the first payment's interest and principal split.
common_mistakes: Using the annual rate as the monthly rate on a monthly loan.
Multiplying the payment by the number of payments and calling the difference 'interest this year'.
Forgetting fees, insurance or a balloon payment the question mentions.
Rounding the payment before computing total interest.

tools.label: Common-size and trend
tools.what: Several years of income-statement figures as common-size percentages, an index and compound growth.
tools.formula: Common-size % = line / revenue; index = period value / base value x 100; CAGR = (end / start)^(1 / periods) - 1.
steps: Enter the periods in order, starting with the base year.
Enter revenue, cost of sales, operating expenses and net income for every period.
Read each line as a share of revenue in the latest period.
Read the index against the base year and the compound growth across the whole span.
common_mistakes: Comparing a 12-month period with a shorter prior period.
Confusing the latest period-on-period growth with the compound rate.
Using cost of sales as the common-size base instead of revenue.
Reading a CAGR as the path of growth; it uses only the first and last values.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Weighted summary
tools.what: Summarise scores with the design weights you supply, stating the weighting rule.
tools.need: the values you want to weigh and the weights you are declaring
tools.formula: Weighted mean = sum(weight x value) / sum(weight); design effect = (n - 1) / (n_effective - 1).
steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.
Read the weighted mean and the weighted standard deviation.
Read the effective sample size: how many unweighted observations your weights are worth.
common_mistakes: Entering the values and the weights in a different order.
Leaving the weight kind undeclared, so the two standard deviations cannot be told apart.
Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tools.label: Missing-data bounds
tools.what: Bound how far the missing values could move the mean, without imputing them.
tools.formula: The mean is bounded by valuing every missing observation at the minimum and at the maximum observed value; the bound width shows how much the missing data could move it.
steps: Enter the observations you have, leaving missing values blank or marking their codes.
Declare the missing-data mechanism you believe applies; it is recorded, not verified.
Read the complete-case mean and the worst-case bounds.
Report the bound beside the estimate, not instead of it.
common_mistakes: Treating the bound as a confidence interval.
Assuming the missing values are random without evidence.
Dropping incomplete rows and reporting the mean as if nothing were missing.
Using a missing code as a real observation.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Spearman rank correlation
tools.what: Record the rank association between two variables without assuming a linear shape.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Linear regression (HC3)
tools.what: The same regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
tools.formula: The same OLS coefficients with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
steps: Fit the same model as OLS.
Read the robust standard errors and their tests.
Compare with the ordinary OLS errors to see whether heteroskedasticity mattered.
Keep the model specification fixed when comparing.
common_mistakes: Thinking robust errors fix a misspecified model.
Comparing robust errors with a different sample or specification.
Using HC3 as a substitute for checking outliers.
Reporting robust errors without saying which correction was used.

tools.label: Welch two-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare two group means without assuming equal variances.
tools.formula: t = (mean A - mean B) / standard error of the difference, without assuming equal variances.
steps: Check the two groups are independent.
Read the difference, the interval and the p-value together.
Report the effect size, not only significance.
common_mistakes: Treating a small p-value as a large effect.
Using a paired test for independent groups.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Mann-Whitney U test
tools.what: Compare two groups by rank when the distributional assumption is not met.

tools.label: Paired t-test
tools.what: Compare paired before/after measurements on the same units.

tools.label: One-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare a sample mean with a declared target.

tools.label: One-way ANOVA
tools.what: Compare three or more group means and record the effect size and checks.
tools.formula: F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
steps: Check the groups are independent.
Read the F test and the effect size.
Use a post-hoc test before naming which groups differ.
common_mistakes: Running several t-tests instead of one ANOVA.
Naming the winning group from the omnibus test alone.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
tools.what: Compare three or more groups by rank, the non-parametric alternative to ANOVA.

tools.label: Two-way ANOVA
tools.what: Record the two main effects and their interaction with the frozen checks.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Post-hoc pairwise tests
tools.what: Compare group pairs after a significant omnibus test, with the correction declared.

tools.label: Multiple-comparison correction
tools.what: Correct a declared family of tests and show the adjusted decisions.

tools.label: Logistic regression
tools.what: Fit a declared binary-outcome model and record coefficients and fit checks.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Market equilibrium
tools.what: Find the equilibrium price and quantity from declared linear demand and supply, with consumer and producer surplus.
tools.formula: Qd = a - bP and Qs = c + dP; set Qd = Qs to find P*, then Q* = a - bP*.
steps: Write demand as Qd = a - bP and supply as Qs = c + dP.
Set Qd = Qs and solve for the equilibrium price P*.
Substitute P* into either curve to get the equilibrium quantity Q*.
Consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above P*; producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below P*.
common_mistakes: Using the inverse form P = a - bQ without rearranging it to Q = a - bP.
Forgetting to check that P* and Q* are positive.
Adding the two surplus triangles when one lies below the price axis.

tools.label: Price elasticity of demand
tools.what: Measure the arc elasticity between two price-quantity observations and see what happens to revenue.
tools.formula: E = (% change in Q) / (% change in P), using the midpoint (arc) formula.
steps: Compute the change in quantity divided by the average quantity.
Compute the change in price divided by the average price.
Divide the first percentage change by the second.
Compare the absolute value with one and read the revenue change.
common_mistakes: Using the slope of the inverse demand curve instead of the percentage changes.
Calling a negative elasticity inelastic because the sign is negative.
Mixing percentages and decimals in the same calculation.
Using the point formula for a discrete change.

tools.label: Tax incidence and deadweight loss
tools.what: Split a per-unit tax between buyers and sellers and record the revenue and deadweight loss.
tools.formula: Consumer price Pc and producer price Ps satisfy Pc - Ps = t; the burden split follows the slopes.
steps: Find the no-tax equilibrium first.
Shift the supply curve up by the per-unit tax.
Read the new consumer price and producer price.
Split the tax between the two sides, then compute revenue and deadweight loss.
common_mistakes: Assuming the side that hands the tax to the government bears the burden.
Forgetting the tax wedge between the buyer's price and the seller's price.
Reporting the tax as a percentage when the input is per unit.

tools.label: Price ceilings and floors
tools.what: See the shortage, surplus and deadweight loss created by a declared price control.
tools.formula: At the control price, compare quantity demanded with quantity supplied; the short side determines quantity traded.
steps: Find the free-market equilibrium.
Decide whether the ceiling is below it or the floor is above it.
At the control price, compute quantity demanded and quantity supplied.
Report the shortage or surplus, the quantity traded and the deadweight loss.
common_mistakes: Treating a non-binding control as if it changed the market.
Reversing shortage and surplus.
Using the long side of the market as quantity traded.

tools.label: Market concentration (HHI)
tools.what: Compute HHI, CR4 and the equivalent number of firms from declared firm revenues.
tools.formula: HHI = sum of squared percentage market shares; CR4 = sum of the four largest shares.
steps: Add the declared revenues to get the market total.
Divide each firm's revenue by the total and multiply by one hundred.
Square each share and add them for the HHI.
Add the four largest shares for CR4; the equivalent number of firms is 10,000 divided by the HHI.
common_mistakes: Entering fractions when the HHI expects percentage shares.
Using total corporate revenue instead of sales in the relevant market.
Treating the HHI as a legal conclusion rather than a descriptive measure.

tools.label: Cost curves
tools.what: Average, average variable, average fixed and marginal cost at a declared quantity, with profit and a shutdown test if you supply a price.
tools.formula: TC = FC + bQ + cQ^2; AC = TC / Q; MC = b + 2cQ.
steps: Enter fixed cost and the linear and quadratic variable-cost terms.
Choose the quantity at which to evaluate the costs.
Read AC, AVC, AFC and MC together; MC crosses AC at the minimum of AC.
If you supply a price, compare it with the minimum AVC to test shutdown.
common_mistakes: Using total cost where the formula needs fixed cost.
Confusing marginal cost with average cost.
Forgetting the quadratic term when computing marginal cost.
Shutting down whenever profit is negative, even when price covers average variable cost.

tools.label: Profit maximisation
tools.what: Find the output and price where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, with profit, markup and the Lerner index.
tools.formula: Set MR = MC: a - 2bQ = c + 2dQ, then P = a - bQ.
steps: Write demand as P = a - bQ, so marginal revenue is a - 2bQ.
Write marginal cost from the cost function as c + 2dQ.
Set MR = MC and solve for Q.
Substitute Q back into demand for P, then compute revenue, cost and profit.
common_mistakes: Setting price equal to marginal cost; that is the competitive outcome, not the monopoly optimum.
Using the demand slope instead of twice the demand slope for marginal revenue.
Thinking fixed cost changes the profit-maximising quantity; it changes profit, not the optimum.
Reporting the Lerner index as a percentage without checking its scale.

tools.label: Markup and Lerner index
tools.what: Measure the markup and Lerner index from a price and marginal cost, and the implied demand elasticity.
tools.formula: Lerner index = (P - MC) / P; markup = P - MC; implied elasticity = 1 / Lerner.
steps: Enter the price and the marginal cost at the same quantity.
Subtract marginal cost from price for the markup.
Divide the markup by price for the Lerner index.
If the index is positive, take its inverse for the implied demand elasticity.
common_mistakes: Using average cost instead of marginal cost.
Reading a high markup as proof of consumer harm or a legal violation.
Forgetting that the implied elasticity is model-conditional.

tools.label: Price discrimination
tools.what: Set third-degree prices and quantities in two separated markets.
tools.formula: Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost separately in each market.
steps: Write each market's linear demand.
Set MR = MC in each market for its quantity.
Substitute back for each price.
Add revenues and profits across the two markets.
common_mistakes: Setting one price for both markets.
Ignoring that the markets must be separated and resale impossible.
Using average cost instead of marginal cost.

tools.label: Cournot duopoly
tools.what: Find the two-firm Cournot quantities, price and profits.
steps: Write each firm's best response to the other's quantity.
Solve the two best responses simultaneously.
Substitute the quantities into demand for the price.
Compute each firm's profit.
common_mistakes: Using the monopoly quantity for each firm.
Forgetting the 3b denominator in the solution.
Ignoring the case where one firm is priced out.

tools.label: Nash equilibrium (2x2)
tools.what: Find the pure-strategy Nash equilibria of a declared 2x2 game.
tools.formula: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when neither player can gain by switching strategy alone.
steps: Enter each player's four payoffs in the declared cell order.
For each cell, check the row player's alternative and the column player's alternative.
Flag the cells where neither can gain.
Read the number of pure-strategy equilibria.
common_mistakes: Looking for the highest joint payoff instead of no unilateral gain.
Missing a second equilibrium in a coordination game.
Treating a payoff tie as a non-equilibrium.

tools.label: Panel fixed effects
tools.what: Estimate the within-entity slope from a balanced panel with entity fixed effects.
tools.formula: Within slope = sum of within-entity (x - entity mean x)(y - entity mean y) / sum of within-entity (x - entity mean x)^2.
steps: Check the panel is balanced: every entity has the same periods.
Subtract each entity's mean from its x and y.
Regress the demeaned y on the demeaned x.
Read the within R-squared and degrees of freedom.
common_mistakes: Using pooled OLS and calling it a fixed-effects estimate.
Including a time-invariant regressor, which the within transformation absorbs.
Ignoring clustering when interpreting precision.

tools.label: Instrumental variables
tools.what: Estimate a just-identified IV slope from one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument.
tools.formula: Just-identified IV slope = cov(z, y) / cov(z, x); first stage = cov(z, x) / var(z).
steps: Check the instrument varies and is correlated with the endogenous regressor.
Compute the covariance ratio for the IV slope.
Read the first-stage slope and the OLS slope for comparison.
State the exclusion restriction explicitly.
common_mistakes: Treating a relevant instrument as a valid one; relevance is not exogeneity.
Ignoring weak-instrument problems.
Reading the IV estimate as causal without defending the design.

tools.label: Regression discontinuity
tools.what: Estimate the jump at a cutoff with a local linear fit on each side.
tools.formula: RDD estimate = right-side intercept at the cutoff - left-side intercept at the cutoff.
steps: Choose the cutoff and a bandwidth.
Keep observations within the bandwidth on each side.
Fit a separate local linear line on each side.
Read the jump in intercepts at the cutoff.
common_mistakes: Using a global polynomial through the whole sample.
Choosing the bandwidth after seeing the estimate.
Ignoring manipulation or another discontinuity at the cutoff.

tools.label: Probit model
tools.what: Fit a binary probit with one predictor and read the marginal effect at the mean.
tools.formula: P(y = 1) = Phi(intercept + slope x x); the marginal effect at the mean is phi(intercept + slope x mean x) x slope.
steps: Check the outcome is binary and both outcomes occur.
Fit the latent-index probit by maximum likelihood.
Read the slope and intercept on the latent scale.
Evaluate the marginal effect at the mean of the predictor.
common_mistakes: Reading the slope as a constant probability effect.
Ignoring separation or near-separation.
Comparing probit and logit coefficients directly without scaling.

tools.label: GDP and national income
tools.what: Build GDP by the expenditure approach, then GNP, NNP, net exports, GDP per capita and real GDP.
tools.formula: GDP = C + I + G + X - M; GNP = GDP + net factor income; NNP = GNP - depreciation.
steps: Add household consumption, investment and government spending.
Add exports and subtract imports.
Add net factor income for GNP, then subtract depreciation for NNP.
If you supply a population or deflator, read GDP per capita or real GDP.
common_mistakes: Adding imports instead of subtracting them.
Double counting intermediate goods as if they were final expenditure.
Confusing GDP with GNP; the difference is net factor income from abroad.
Using a deflator as a percentage rather than an index with a base of 100.

tools.label: Growth rate and CAGR
tools.what: Compute total growth, the compound annual growth rate and the rule-of-72 doubling time.
tools.formula: CAGR = (end / start)^(1 / periods) - 1; doubling time is about 72 / (CAGR x 100).
steps: Enter the start value, end value and number of periods.
Read total growth as the proportional change.
Read CAGR as the constant rate that compounds the start to the end.
Use the rule of 72 only as an approximation for the doubling time.
common_mistakes: Averaging yearly growth rates instead of compounding them.
Confusing total growth with the annual compound rate.
Using the rule of 72 at very high or negative growth rates.
Forgetting to adjust for population when the question is per-capita growth.

tools.label: Inflation and real interest
tools.what: Compute inflation from two CPI values, the exact and approximate real interest rate, and real wage growth.
tools.formula: Inflation = (CPI end - CPI start) / CPI start; real interest = (1 + nominal) / (1 + inflation) - 1.
steps: Enter the two CPI values.
Divide their difference by the starting CPI for inflation.
If you have a nominal interest rate, apply the Fisher relation for the real rate.
If you have wages, compare their growth with inflation for real wage growth.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the two CPI values and calling the difference the inflation rate.
Using nominal minus inflation at high inflation without saying it is an approximation.
Confusing nominal and real wages.
Treating the CPI as a price level in currency rather than an index.

tools.label: Unemployment and participation
tools.what: Compute the unemployment rate, labour-force participation rate and employment-population ratio.
tools.formula: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force; LFPR = labour force / working-age population.
steps: Enter the labour force, the number employed and the working-age population.
Subtract employment from the labour force for the unemployed.
Divide the unemployed by the labour force for the unemployment rate.
Use the working-age population for participation and the employment ratio.
common_mistakes: Dividing the unemployed by the working-age population instead of the labour force.
Counting discouraged workers as unemployed when they are outside the labour force.
Mixing the participation and employment-ratio denominators.
Treating the unemployment rate as a measure of hardship by itself.

tools.label: Money multiplier
tools.what: Compute the simple and currency-adjusted money multipliers and the implied money supply.
tools.formula: Simple multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; extended = (1 + currency drain) / (reserve ratio + currency drain).
steps: Enter the monetary base and the reserve ratio.
Compute the simple multiplier as the inverse of the reserve ratio.
Add the currency drain for the extended multiplier.
Multiply the base by the multiplier for the implied money supply.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the currency drain, which lowers the multiplier.
Assuming banks hold no excess reserves.
Confusing the monetary base with the money supply.
Treating the multiplier as a forecast rather than an identity.

tools.label: Fiscal multipliers
tools.what: Compute the government-spending, tax and balanced-budget multipliers and the output change from a declared fiscal package.
tools.formula: Government multiplier = 1 / (1 - MPC(1 - t)); tax multiplier = -MPC / (1 - MPC(1 - t)).
steps: Enter the marginal propensity to consume and the proportional tax rate.
Compute the denominator 1 - MPC(1 - t).
Read the government-spending, tax and balanced-budget multipliers.
Apply the declared spending and tax changes to get the output change.
common_mistakes: Using 1 / (1 - MPC) when there is an income tax; the tax rate belongs in the denominator.
Thinking the tax multiplier is positive.
Confusing a lump-sum tax change with a change in the tax rate.
Treating the multiplier as an estimated policy effect rather than an identity.

tools.label: Budget balance and debt
tools.what: Compute the overall and primary balances, the debt-to-GDP ratio and the debt-ratio change.
tools.formula: Overall balance = revenue - spending - interest; debt ratio = debt / GDP.
steps: Enter revenue, primary spending, interest, debt and GDP.
Add interest to primary spending for total spending.
Subtract total spending from revenue for the overall balance.
Divide debt by GDP for the debt ratio and apply the interest-growth-primary identity for its change.
common_mistakes: Including interest in primary spending and then adding it again.
Confusing the overall balance with the primary balance.
Treating the debt-ratio change as a forecast rather than an identity.
Using nominal GDP growth without saying it is nominal.

tools.label: Output gap and Okun's law
tools.what: Compute the output gap and the unemployment change implied by a declared Okun coefficient.
tools.formula: Output gap = (actual GDP - potential GDP) / potential GDP; unemployment change = -Okun coefficient x gap.
steps: Enter actual and potential GDP on the same basis.
Compute the proportional output gap.
Apply the declared Okun coefficient for the unemployment change in percentage points.
Add the change to the current unemployment rate.
common_mistakes: Getting the sign wrong: a positive gap lowers unemployment.
Treating potential GDP as observed rather than declared.
Confusing percentage points with percent.

tools.label: Externalities and Pigouvian tax
tools.what: Compare the private market with the social optimum and record the Pigouvian tax and deadweight loss.
tools.formula: Social optimum: demand = private supply + marginal external cost; Pigouvian tax = marginal external cost; DWL = 1/2 x tax x (market quantity - social quantity).
steps: Find the private market equilibrium first.
Add the external cost to private supply to get the social cost.
Solve for the social quantity and compare it with the market quantity.
Read the Pigouvian tax and the deadweight-loss triangle.
common_mistakes: Ignoring the external cost and calling the private equilibrium efficient.
Taxing the market quantity instead of the social quantity.
Confusing the per-unit tax with total external damage.

tools.label: Public goods
tools.what: Find the efficient provision of a public good from two benefit schedules and a cost schedule.
tools.formula: Sum the marginal benefits vertically; set social marginal benefit equal to marginal cost.
steps: Write each person's marginal benefit as a linear schedule.
Add the schedules vertically to get social marginal benefit.
Set it equal to marginal cost and solve for the efficient quantity.
Compare total benefit with total cost.
common_mistakes: Adding the demand curves horizontally, which is the private-good case.
Using one person's marginal benefit as the social benefit.
Forgetting that voluntary contribution generally underprovides.

tools.label: Social welfare functions
tools.what: Compare utilitarian, Rawlsian and Nash welfare for the same incomes.
tools.formula: Utilitarian = sum of incomes; Rawlsian = minimum income; Nash = geometric mean.
steps: Enter the incomes and choose the welfare function.
Read all three welfare values alongside the selected one.
Compare how a transfer changes each criterion.
common_mistakes: Treating the choice of welfare function as an empirical result.
Comparing incomes without an equivalence scale.
Thinking Nash welfare is the same as the sum.

tools.label: Gini coefficient
tools.what: Measure inequality from declared incomes, with the poorest and richest shares.
tools.formula: Gini = (2 x sum of rank-weighted incomes - (n + 1) x total income) / (n x total income).
steps: Sort the incomes from lowest to highest.
Compute the mean and the rank-weighted sum.
Apply the Gini formula; zero means perfect equality.
Read the poorest and richest shares for context.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the Gini by one hundred and calling it a different index.
Using negative incomes, which the method refuses.
Treating the Gini as a full picture of where inequality lies.

tools.label: Poverty measures
tools.what: Compute the headcount, poverty gap and squared gap against a declared poverty line.
tools.formula: Headcount = share below the line; poverty gap = average normalised shortfall over the population.
steps: Choose and declare the poverty line.
Count the incomes below it for the headcount.
Average the normalised shortfall for the gap, and square it for the squared gap.
Read the total shortfall in currency.
common_mistakes: Averaging the gap only over the poor instead of the whole population.
Changing the poverty line after seeing the result.
Confusing the headcount with the depth of poverty.

tools.label: Tax progressivity
tools.what: Compare the top quartile's income share with its tax share.
tools.formula: Progressivity gap = top-quartile tax share - top-quartile income share.
steps: Enter each person's income and tax.
Rank by income and take the top quartile.
Compare its tax share with its income share.
A positive gap means the top pays proportionally more.
common_mistakes: Calling a proportional tax progressive; its gap is zero.
Using the top decile when the method uses the top quartile.
Ignoring tax incidence and behavioural responses.

tools.label: Optimal pollution
tools.what: Find the emission level where marginal damage equals marginal abatement cost, with the pollution tax.
tools.formula: Set marginal damage equal to marginal abatement cost; the pollution tax equals marginal damage at the optimum.
steps: Write marginal damage as rising with emissions.
Write marginal abatement cost as falling with emissions.
Set them equal and solve for optimal emissions.
Read the tax and the total damage.
common_mistakes: Setting marginal abatement cost to zero instead of equal to marginal damage.
Confusing the pollution tax with total damage.
Forgetting that the curves are declared, not estimated.

tools.label: Comparative advantage
tools.what: Find opportunity costs and comparative advantage from two countries' unit labour requirements.
tools.formula: Opportunity cost of good one = hours per unit of good one / hours per unit of good two.
steps: Enter each country's unit labour requirements for both goods.
Compute the opportunity cost of each good in each country.
The lower opportunity cost identifies comparative advantage.
Check that the two countries specialise in different goods.
common_mistakes: Using absolute hours instead of opportunity cost.
Assuming a country cannot have comparative advantage if it is better at both goods.
Forgetting that the two opportunity costs are reciprocals.

tools.label: Tariff welfare
tools.what: Compute the domestic price, imports, tariff revenue and deadweight loss of a small-country tariff.
tools.formula: Domestic price = world price + tariff; imports = quantity demanded - quantity supplied.
steps: Find free-trade imports at the world price.
Add the tariff to get the domestic price.
Compute the new imports and tariff revenue.
Add the production and consumption deadweight-loss triangles.
common_mistakes: Using the world price as the domestic price after the tariff.
Forgetting one of the two deadweight-loss triangles.
Applying small-country results to a large country.

tools.label: Purchasing-power parity
tools.what: Compare a nominal exchange rate with PPP and record the real rate and expected depreciation.
tools.formula: PPP rate = domestic price / foreign price; real exchange rate = nominal x foreign price / domestic price.
steps: Enter the two price levels and the nominal rate as domestic per foreign.
Compute the PPP rate and the real rate.
Read the misalignment: zero means the nominal rate is at PPP.
If inflation rates are supplied, read expected depreciation.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exchange-rate quotation.
Confusing absolute and relative PPP.
Treating PPP as a short-run forecast.

tools.label: Interest-rate parity
tools.what: Compute the covered-interest-parity forward rate and forward premium from two interest rates.
tools.formula: Forward = spot x [(1 + domestic rate) / (1 + foreign rate)]^T.
steps: Enter the spot rate, the two interest rates and the horizon.
Compute the parity forward rate.
Read the forward premium as the interest differential.
If a forward is declared, compare it with parity.
common_mistakes: Using simple interest when the method compounds over the horizon.
Confusing covered and uncovered parity.
Forgetting that the horizon must match the rates.

tools.label: Balance of payments
tools.what: Check the current, capital and financial accounts against the balance-of-payments identity.
tools.formula: Current account + capital account + financial account + errors and omissions = 0.
steps: Enter the three account balances on one sign convention.
Add them, including declared errors and omissions.
A zero net balance closes the identity.
Read the current-account-to-GDP ratio if GDP is supplied.
common_mistakes: Mixing sign conventions across the accounts.
Treating a zero balance as proof of sustainability.
Double counting reserve changes.

tools.label: Human Development Index
tools.what: Compute the HDI from life expectancy, schooling and GNI per capita using the UNDP goalposts.
tools.formula: HDI = geometric mean of the life, education and income indices.
steps: Enter life expectancy, expected and mean schooling, and GNI per capita.
Scale each dimension against the UNDP goalposts.
Take the geometric mean of the three indices.
Read each dimension index to see what drives the result.
common_mistakes: Using a different goalpost set without saying so.
Taking an arithmetic mean instead of the geometric mean.
Mixing currencies or purchasing-power bases in GNI.

tools.label: Expected utility
tools.what: Compute expected value, expected utility, the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.
tools.formula: EV = sum of probability x outcome; EU = sum of probability x utility; the certainty equivalent is the certain amount with the same utility.
steps: Enter the outcomes and probabilities.
Compute the expected value.
Apply the declared utility function for expected utility.
Invert the utility for the certainty equivalent and risk premium.
common_mistakes: Confusing expected value with expected utility.
Using negative wealth with CRRA utility.
Treating the risk premium as an observed fee.

tools.label: Prospect theory
tools.what: Value a gamble around a reference point with loss aversion and probability weighting.
tools.formula: v(gain) = gain^alpha; v(loss) = -loss aversion x loss^beta; probabilities are weighted.
steps: Choose the reference point.
Enter outcomes and probabilities.
Evaluate gains and losses relative to the reference.
Apply the declared loss aversion, curvature and weighting.
common_mistakes: Treating prospect theory as a normative recommendation.
Forgetting that the reference point changes the value.
Mixing the gain and loss curvature parameters.

tools.label: Real wage and labour market
tools.what: Compute the real wage, wage share of productivity and labour-market tightness.
tools.formula: Real wage = nominal wage / (CPI / 100); wage share = real wage / labour productivity.
steps: Enter the nominal wage, CPI and productivity.
Deflate the nominal wage by the price index.
Divide the real wage by productivity for the wage share.
If vacancies and unemployment are supplied, read tightness.
common_mistakes: Using the nominal wage as if it were real.
Dividing by the CPI instead of CPI/100.
Confusing the wage share with the labour share of GDP.

tools.label: Difference-in-differences
tools.what: Estimate a two-group, two-period treatment effect from four declared means.
tools.formula: DiD = (treated post - treated pre) - (control post - control pre).
steps: Enter the four group-period means.
Compute the treated change and the control change.
Subtract the control change from the treated change.
State the parallel-trends assumption explicitly.
common_mistakes: Comparing post-treatment means only.
Ignoring the parallel-trends assumption.
Confusing DiD with a simple before-and-after comparison.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.

tools.label: Currency conversion
tools.what: Convert an amount at a rate you declare; the rate and its source are recorded.
tools.formula: Converted amount = amount x rate, with the rate's provenance recorded.
steps: Enter the amount, the source currency and the target currency.
Declare the rate and where it came from.
Read the converted amount and the recorded rate.
Keep the rate date with the result.
common_mistakes: Multiplying when the quote is the other way up; divide instead.
Using a stale rate without saying so.
Forgetting the target currency's minor units.
Treating a declared rate as a verified market rate.

tools.label: Pricing rules
tools.what: Cost-plus, target-margin, break-even and target-return prices from your cost, volume and rate.
tools.formula: Cost-plus price = unit cost x (1 + markup); margin price = unit cost / (1 - margin); break-even price = total cost / expected units.
steps: Enter the variable cost per unit and the fixed cost for the period.
Enter the volume you expect to sell.
Read the cost-plus price at your markup, then the margin price and the break-even price.
Compare them with what customers in your market actually pay; the method cannot do that part.
common_mistakes: Treating a 40% margin as a 40% markup: a markup on cost always gives a lower price than the same margin on price.
Forgetting fixed costs when pricing a small volume.
Setting a price below variable cost and hoping volume fixes it.
Ignoring what competitors charge in the same market.

tools.label: Demand line and revenue-max price
tools.what: Fit a line to your price and quantity pairs and read the slope, the elasticity and the price that maximises revenue.
tools.formula: q = a + b p, fitted by least squares; elasticity at the mean = b x (mean price / mean quantity).
steps: Collect price-quantity pairs from the same market and period basis.
Enter the prices and the quantity demanded at each price.
Read the slope, the R-squared and the elasticity at the mean price.
If the slope is negative, read the revenue-maximising price on the fitted line.
common_mistakes: Treating the fitted line as an identified demand curve.
Mixing observations from different periods or markets.
Extrapolating far outside the observed price range.
Ignoring that price and quantity are jointly determined.

tools.label: Cost-benefit analysis
tools.what: Compare the present value of programme costs and benefits under declared assumptions.
tools.formula: NPV = PV(benefits) - PV(costs); BCR = PV(benefits) / PV(costs).
steps: Discount each period's costs and benefits at the declared rate.
Subtract present-value costs from present-value benefits.
Divide benefits by costs for the benefit-cost ratio.
common_mistakes: Choosing the discount rate after seeing the result.
Counting a transfer as a benefit or a cost.
Comparing projects with different horizons without saying so.

tools.label: Cost-effectiveness analysis
tools.what: Compare cost per unit of effect across options, with the effect measure declared.
tools.formula: ICER = (cost of option - cost of comparator) / (effect of option - effect of comparator).
steps: Name the comparator first.
Compute the incremental cost and the incremental effect for each other option.
Divide the cost difference by the effect difference.
common_mistakes: Comparing options on different effect scales.
Ignoring a dominant option because it has no finite ratio.
Choosing the comparator after seeing the ratios.

tools.label: Social return on investment
tools.what: Record the SROI ratio from declared social value, investment and attribution assumptions.
tools.formula: SROI = PV(social benefits) / investment.
steps: Discount the declared social benefits.
Divide their present value by the declared investment.
State the attribution and deadweight assumptions explicitly.
common_mistakes: Treating an unmonetised outcome as if it had been valued.
Omitting deadweight, attribution or displacement adjustments.
Presenting the ratio as assurance.

tools.label: Net present value
tools.what: Discount a project's cash flows at a declared rate and record the NPV with its checks.
tools.need: the outlay, the later cash flows, and the hurdle rate you will justify
tools.formula: NPV = sum of CF_t / (1 + r)^t, with the first cash flow at t = 0 and undiscounted.
steps: List the cash flows in order, starting with the negative outlay at t = 0.
Choose the discount rate that matches the project's risk.
Discount each flow and add them.
Compare the result with zero; a positive NPV clears the hurdle at that rate.
common_mistakes: Discounting the t = 0 outlay, which removes one period of discounting.
Using accounting profit instead of cash flow.
Entering the rate as 10 instead of 0.10.
Comparing NPVs of projects with different lives without an equivalent-annual measure.

tools.label: DCF valuation (year-end)
tools.what: Value a business or project from forecast free cash flows and a declared discount rate.
tools.formula: EV = sum of FCF_t / (1 + r)^t + TV / (1 + r)^n; TV = FCF_n(1 + g) / (r - g).
steps: Enter the free cash flows for the explicit forecast.
Enter the discount rate that matches the cash flows.
If the business continues, declare a terminal growth rate below the discount rate.
Read the explicit present value, the terminal present value and their sum.
common_mistakes: Using a growth rate at or above the discount rate.
Discounting equity cash flows at WACC, or enterprise cash flows at the cost of equity.
Forgetting that the terminal value usually dominates the answer.
Forecasting cash flows inside the method; they are your declaration.

tools.label: Break-even point
tools.what: Solve the break-even quantity from fixed cost, price and variable cost.
tools.formula: Break-even quantity = fixed cost / (price - variable cost per unit); break-even revenue = quantity x price; margin of safety = expected units - break-even units.
steps: Subtract variable cost from price to get the unit contribution and the contribution-margin ratio.
Divide fixed cost by the unit contribution for the break-even quantity.
Multiply by the price for the break-even revenue.
If you declare an expected volume, read the margin of safety; a profit target gives its volume.
common_mistakes: Using total cost instead of fixed cost.
Forgetting that a price below variable cost has no break-even.
Mixing per-unit and total figures.
Reporting a margin of safety against a budget you did not declare.

tools.label: Multi-product break-even
tools.what: Find the sales mix at which several products together cover their fixed costs.
tools.formula: Weighted contribution = sum(mix weight x unit contribution); break-even units = fixed cost / weighted contribution.
steps: Compute each product's unit contribution.
Weight the contributions by the declared sales mix.
Divide fixed cost by the weighted contribution.
Split the break-even units back across the mix.
common_mistakes: Using a simple average instead of the mix-weighted contribution.
Letting the mix change while claiming one break-even point.
Ignoring capacity limits.

tools.label: Unit economics
tools.what: The margin per customer, the cost to win one, its payback and lifetime value.
tools.formula: Contribution margin = price - variable cost; LTV = margin / churn; CAC payback = acquisition cost / margin.
steps: Enter the price and the variable cost per unit or customer.
Enter the acquisition cost and, if you know it, the churn rate.
Read the margin, the payback period and the LTV/CAC ratio.
Check that price and cost are for the same period.
common_mistakes: Using gross profit instead of contribution margin.
Entering churn as a percentage (5) instead of a decimal (0.05).
Comparing an undiscounted LTV with a discounted cost.
Treating a single churn rate as a retention curve.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Welch two-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare two group means without assuming equal variances.
tools.formula: t = (mean A - mean B) / standard error of the difference, without assuming equal variances.
steps: Check the two groups are independent.
Read the difference, the interval and the p-value together.
Report the effect size, not only significance.
common_mistakes: Treating a small p-value as a large effect.
Using a paired test for independent groups.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: One-way ANOVA
tools.what: Compare three or more group means and record the effect size and checks.
tools.formula: F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
steps: Check the groups are independent.
Read the F test and the effect size.
Use a post-hoc test before naming which groups differ.
common_mistakes: Running several t-tests instead of one ANOVA.
Naming the winning group from the omnibus test alone.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Market size (TAM, SAM, SOM)
tools.what: Size the whole market, the part you can serve and the part you can win from a population, an annual spend and two shares you declare.
tools.formula: TAM = customers x annual spend; SAM = TAM x serviceable share; SOM = SAM x obtainable share.
steps: Count the customers in the market you are describing, or use a population and a spend figure you can defend.
Multiply by the average annual spend for the total addressable market.
Apply the share of that market you can physically serve, then the share of that market you can win.
Check that each share is below one and that SOM is smaller than SAM, which is smaller than TAM.
common_mistakes: Presenting SOM as if it were the whole market.
Using a national population when the shop serves one barangay.
Mixing a monthly spend with an annual population figure.
Calling the shares evidence: they are assumptions unless you cite a source.

tools.label: Sales and profit projection
tools.what: Project volume, revenue, costs and profit period by period from a starting volume and a growth rate.
tools.formula: Units_t = units_1 x (1 + g)^(t-1); revenue = units x price; profit = revenue - units x unit cost - fixed cost.
steps: Enter the units you expect in the first period, the price and the unit variable cost.
Enter the fixed cost for one period and the growth you assume per period.
Declare how many periods the plan covers.
Read each period's units, revenue and profit, and the totals across the horizon.
common_mistakes: Applying growth to revenue while leaving volume unchanged.
Entering an annual fixed cost on a monthly plan.
Assuming a growth rate forever without a capacity limit.
Treating a projection as a forecast the evidence supports.

tools.label: Cap table and dilution
tools.what: Post-money value, price per share, new shares, investor and founder percentages and dilution for one round.
tools.formula: Post-money = pre-money + investment; price per share = pre-money / existing shares; new shares = investment / price; investor % = new shares / fully diluted shares.
steps: Enter the agreed pre-money valuation and the amount invested.
Enter all shares outstanding before the round.
If an option pool is part of the deal, declare it as a share of the fully diluted company.
Read the post-money value, the price per share, the new shares and each holder's percentage.
common_mistakes: Confusing pre-money and post-money values.
Forgetting the option pool when quoting the investor's percentage.
Treating a convertible note as if it were a priced round.
Reading the arithmetic as a fair valuation.

tools.label: Sales funnel and conversion
tools.what: Enter how many people reached each stage and read the conversion, the drop-off and the cost of winning a customer.
tools.formula: Stage conversion = count at the next stage / count at this stage; overall conversion = last count / first count.
steps: List the stages in the order a customer meets them.
Enter how many people reached each stage in the same period.
Read each stage's conversion, the overall conversion and the drop-off.
If you declare the spend, read the acquisition cost per customer.
common_mistakes: Reordering stages so a smaller count comes first.
Mixing periods between stages.
Counting the same customer twice in one stage.
Reading a conversion difference as statistical proof.

tools.label: Cohort retention
tools.what: Follow groups of customers who started together and read retention, churn and the average customer life.
tools.formula: Period retention = retained customers in that period / starting customers, pooled across cohorts; average lifetime = the sum of the period retention rates.
steps: Enter the number of customers in each cohort when it started.
Enter how many of each cohort were still buying in each later period.
Keep every cohort's row the same length; leave out a period a cohort has not reached.
Read the pooled retention curve, the churn and the average lifetime.
common_mistakes: Zero-filling a period the cohort has not reached yet.
Mixing revenue retention with customer retention.
Averaging cohort rates without weighting by cohort size.
Reading a lifetime as a forecast.

tools.label: Demand line and revenue-max price
tools.what: Fit a line to your price and quantity pairs and read the slope, the elasticity and the price that maximises revenue.
tools.formula: q = a + b p, fitted by least squares; elasticity at the mean = b x (mean price / mean quantity).
steps: Collect price-quantity pairs from the same market and period basis.
Enter the prices and the quantity demanded at each price.
Read the slope, the R-squared and the elasticity at the mean price.
If the slope is negative, read the revenue-maximising price on the fitted line.
common_mistakes: Treating the fitted line as an identified demand curve.
Mixing observations from different periods or markets.
Extrapolating far outside the observed price range.
Ignoring that price and quantity are jointly determined.

tools.label: Purchase intent
tools.what: Turn weighted survey answers into an expected buying rate, projected buyers and projected revenue.
tools.formula: Intent rate = (definitely x w1 + probably x w2 + maybe x w3 + never x w4) / respondents; projected buyers = population x intent rate.
steps: Enter how many respondents gave each answer.
Declare the weight each answer carries, or use the stated defaults.
Read the weighted intent rate.
If you declare the population and the price, read projected buyers and projected revenue.
common_mistakes: Treating stated intent as a sale.
Using weights without saying where they came from.
Projecting onto a population the sample does not represent.
Forgetting that the sample size limits the precision.

tools.label: Sales from market share
tools.what: Target revenue and units from a declared market size, share and price.
tools.formula: Target revenue = market size x target share; target units = revenue / price.
steps: Enter the annual market size in your currency.
Declare the share you plan to win as a fraction.
Enter your price per unit.
Read the target revenue and units; carry them into the sales projection.
common_mistakes: Entering a percentage as 10 instead of 0.10.
Using a national market for a single shop.
Treating a planned share as evidence of demand.
Forgetting that revenue is market size times share, not units times price.

tools.label: Projected statements
tools.what: Projected income statement, cash flow and balance sheet from your declared drivers, with the balance check.
tools.formula: Net income = revenue x margin - operating costs - depreciation - interest - tax; cash = opening + operating + investing + financing flows; assets = liabilities + equity.
steps: Enter revenue for each period and the gross margin.
Enter operating costs, depreciation, interest and principal repayment.
Enter tax, working-capital days and the opening balance sheet.
Read the income statement, cash flow and balance sheet; fix any period that does not balance.
common_mistakes: Leaving an opening balance sheet that does not balance.
Forgetting depreciation in the cash flow (it is added back, not paid).
Mixing a monthly revenue list with annual days.
Treating the projection as a forecast rather than declared drivers.

tools.label: Price and volume sensitivity
tools.what: Profit across declared price and volume changes, with the base case.
tools.formula: Profit = (price x (1 + price change) - unit cost) x units x (1 + volume change) - fixed cost.
steps: Enter the base price, units, unit variable cost and fixed cost.
Declare one to five price changes and volume changes as fractions.
Read the base profit and each cell.
Use the table to show how much the result moves, not to choose a scenario.
common_mistakes: Entering 10 for a 10% change instead of 0.10.
Changing costs in a table that only varies price and volume.
Reading a cell as a probability-weighted outcome.
Forgetting that price and volume often move together.

tools.label: Depreciation schedule
tools.what: The period charge, accumulated depreciation and carrying amount, straight line or declining balance.
tools.formula: Straight line: (cost - salvage) / life each period. Declining balance: carrying amount x rate, with the final period plugged to salvage.
steps: Enter the asset's cost, its expected salvage value and the useful life.
Choose straight line or declining balance.
Read each period's charge, the accumulated depreciation and the carrying amount.
Use the period charges in the projected statements.
common_mistakes: Depreciating below the salvage value.
Using a tax depreciation rate as the accounting life.
Forgetting that the final declining-balance period is a plug.
Treating depreciation as a cash payment.

tools.label: Start-up capital and amount to raise
tools.what: Add set-up costs, working capital and a contingency, subtract what is already committed, and record the funding gap.
tools.formula: Requirement = (set-up costs + working capital) x (1 + contingency rate); amount to raise = requirement - owner equity - loan.
steps: List the one-off costs to open: equipment, fit-out, permits, deposits and initial stock.
Add the cash needed to operate before receipts cover the costs.
Add a contingency you can justify, as a percentage of that base.
Subtract the owner's cash and any loan already approved to get the amount still to raise.
common_mistakes: Leaving out working capital, so the business opens and cannot pay its first bills.
Counting a loan you have only applied for as committed funding.
Adding the contingency to each line instead of to the total.
Forgetting that the amount to raise is after your own contribution.

tools.label: Cash runway and funding gap
tools.what: Months of cash left at a declared monthly burn, the lowest balance and the cash needed over your horizon.
tools.formula: Runway = opening cash / monthly burn (no growth); with growth g, runway = ln(1 - opening x g / burn) / ln(1 + g) for a negative flow.
steps: Enter the cash you have now.
Enter the monthly net cash flow: cash received minus cash paid. A loss is a negative number.
If the flow changes each month, declare the monthly growth you assume.
Read the runway in months, the lowest balance and the funding gap over your horizon.
common_mistakes: Using profit instead of cash: a receivable is not cash in the bank.
Entering a positive flow and expecting a runway.
Forgetting loan repayments and owner drawings in the monthly flow.
Treating the runway as a forecast rather than arithmetic on one declared flow.

Forgetting fixed costs when pricing a small volume.
Setting a price below variable cost and hoping volume fixes it.
Ignoring what competitors charge in the same market.

tools.label: Return on investment
tools.what: ROI and the annualised return from a declared investment and net gain.
tools.formula: ROI = net gain / total investment; annualised ROI = (1 + ROI)^(1/years) - 1.
steps: Enter the total amount invested.
Enter the total gain net of that investment over the whole holding period.
Read the return, and the annualised return if you declare the years.
Compare it with the return you could get elsewhere before you call it good.
common_mistakes: Entering the final value instead of the net gain.
Entering one year's gain when the holding period is longer.
Annualising a loss of 100% or more, which has no real rate.
Calling ROI a discounted measure: it ignores when the cash arrives.

Read the margin, the payback period and the LTV/CAC ratio.
